title: Pronouns
description: Learn pronouns for Grade 6: personal, possessive, reflexive, demonstrative, interrogative, indefinite and relative pronouns — with bilingual notes, examples, practice and tests.

topics.title: Personal Pronouns: Subject vs Object
topics.concept:
Subject pronouns do the action and usually come before the verb: I, you, he, she, it, we, they.

Object pronouns receive the action and come after the verb or a preposition: me, you, him, her, it, us, them.

The classic test: ask who is doing the verb (subject) and who is it done to (object).

  • He called her. (He = subject, her = object)
  • Give the keys to them. (after preposition 'to' → object)

examples.problem: Choose: (I / Me) and my friend went out.
examples.solution: My friend and I went out. — 'I' is the subject doing the action. (Polite order also puts the other person first.)
him — it receives the action, so use the object pronoun.

recap: Subject pronouns (I, he, she, we, they) do the action
Object pronouns (me, him, her, us, them) receive the action
After a preposition (to, for, with) always use the object form

topics.title: Possessives, Reflexives & Demonstratives
topics.concept:
Possessive adjectives come before a noun: my book, your pen, their house.

Possessive pronouns stand alone (no noun after): This book is mine. That pen is yours.

Reflexive pronouns end in -self/-selves and point back to the subject: myself, yourself, himself, herself, itself, ourselves, yourselves, themselves — She hurt herself.

Demonstrative pronouns point things out: this, that (singular), these, those (plural).

examples.problem: Possessive adjective or pronoun? This is ___ (my / mine) seat.
examples.solution: my — a noun ('seat') follows, so use the possessive adjective.
itself — the action points back to the subject (the cat), so use a reflexive pronoun.

recap: Possessive adjective + noun (my book); possessive pronoun stands alone (mine)
Reflexive pronouns (-self/-selves) point back to the subject

topics.title: Interrogative, Indefinite & Relative Pronouns
topics.concept:
Interrogative pronouns ask questions: who, whom, whose, which, what.

Indefinite pronouns refer to no particular person/thing: someone, anyone, everyone, nobody, each, both, all, many, few. Most are singular and take a singular verb: Everyone is here.

Relative pronouns join clauses and refer back to a noun: who (people), which (things), that (both) — The girl who won is my friend.

examples.solution: has — 'everyone' is singular, so it takes a singular verb.

examples.problem: Pick the relative pronoun: The book ___ I read was great.
examples.solution: that (or 'which') — it refers to the thing 'book' and joins the clauses.

recap: Interrogatives ask: who, whom, whose, which, what
Most indefinite pronouns (everyone, nobody, each) are singular
Relatives join clauses: who (people), which (things), that (both)

questions.q: Choose the subject pronoun: '___ is my teacher.'
questions.explanation: A subject pronoun ('He') does the action.

questions.q: Fill in: 'I gave the gift to ___.'
questions.explanation: After 'to', use the object pronoun 'her'.

questions.q: Which is a possessive adjective?
questions.explanation: 'their' comes before a noun — a possessive adjective.

questions.q: 'The cat licked ___ fur.'
questions.explanation: 'its' is the possessive form (no apostrophe).

questions.q: Reflexive pronoun for 'I':
questions.explanation: The reflexive of 'I' is 'myself'.

questions.q: Choose the correct sentence.
questions.explanation: After 'between' use object pronouns: 'you and me'.

questions.q: 'Somebody ___ left a bag here.'
questions.explanation: 'Somebody' is singular and takes 'has'.

questions.q: Which is an interrogative pronoun?
questions.explanation: 'whom' is used to ask questions about the object.

questions.q: Demonstrative pronoun for far + plural:
questions.explanation: 'those' points to plural things that are far.

questions.q: 'The student ___ won the prize is here.' (relative)
questions.explanation: 'who' refers to a person doing the action.

questions.q: Pick the correct object pronoun: 'They invited ___.'
questions.explanation: 'us' receives the action of inviting.

questions.q: 'Neither of the boys ___ ready.'
questions.explanation: 'Neither' is singular and takes 'is'.

questions.q: Spot the error: 'My friend and me visited the museum.'
questions.explanation: Subjects need 'My friend and I'.

questions.q: Choose the correct option: 'It was ___ who broke the vase.'
questions.explanation: After the linking verb 'was', the subject pronoun 'he' is used in formal English.

questions.q: Identify the error: 'Each of the girls have submitted their project.'
questions.explanation: 'Each' is singular: 'has submitted'.

questions.q: Fill in correctly: 'The committee published ___ report.'
questions.explanation: Acting as one unit, the collective noun takes 'its'.

questions.q: Which sentence is correct?
options: He is taller than I am.
Both A and B are acceptable.
questions.explanation: 'than I am' is formal; 'than me' is accepted in everyday English.

questions.q: Choose the right relative pronoun: 'This is the boy ___ I met yesterday.'
questions.explanation: As the object of 'met', 'whom' is correct in formal usage.

questions.q: Rearrange: 'yourself / did / you / it / ?'
questions.explanation: 'Did you do it yourself?' is the correct emphatic question.

questions.q: Pick the error: 'Everyone must bring their own pen.'
questions.explanation: Singular 'their' after 'everyone' is now widely accepted; strict grammar prefers 'his or her'.

outcomes: Explain what a pronoun does and why we use one
Tell apart possessive pronouns and possessive adjectives (mine vs my)
Use reflexive, demonstrative, interrogative and indefinite pronouns
Fix common pronoun errors such as 'between you and I'

intro.en: A pronoun is a word used in place of a noun so we don't repeat the noun again and again. Instead of "Ravi took Ravi's bag because Ravi was late," we say "Ravi took his bag because he was late."
intro.hi: सर्वनाम (Pronoun) वह शब्द है जो संज्ञा के स्थान पर प्रयोग होता है, ताकि एक ही नाम बार-बार न दोहराना पड़े। "Ravi took Ravi's bag because Ravi was late" के बजाय हम कहते हैं "Ravi took his bag because he was late."

real_life.situation:
Your mother calls out:

Mother: Where is your brother? Tell him dinner is ready.

You: He is in his room. I'll call him.
real_life.why: We never repeat 'brother' three times. He (subject), him (object) and his (possessive) all stand in for the same noun — that is the whole job of a pronoun.

rule_box.formula: Subject pronoun = doer · Object pronoun = receiver
rule_box.example: She (subject) gave the book to me (object). It is mine (possessive).

words.meaning: the noun a pronoun refers to

quick_test.explanation: Reflexive pronouns (myself, herself) point the action back to the subject.

common_mistakes.wrong: Between you and I, it's a secret.
common_mistakes.right: Between you and me, it's a secret.
common_mistakes.note: After a preposition (between) use the object pronoun 'me'.
The doers of the verb need subject pronouns, and politeness puts 'I' last.
'Everyone' is singular and takes a singular verb.
'its' is the possessive; reflexives have no apostrophe-s.

sentence_correction.correct: Each of the boys has a bag.

reading.passage: Aman and his sister Nisha love painting. They paint together every Sunday. "This brush is mine," says Nisha, "and that one is yours." Aman, who is younger, sometimes spills the colours, but he always cleans the table himself. Everyone in the family enjoys their bright pictures.

questions.q: Which word in the passage is a possessive pronoun?
questions.answer: mine (also 'yours') — it stands alone without a noun after it.

questions.q: Find the reflexive pronoun.
questions.answer: himself — it points the action of cleaning back to Aman.

questions.q: What is the antecedent of 'who' in the passage?
questions.answer: Aman — 'who is younger' refers back to Aman.

speaking: Please give the books to them.
This bag is mine, not yours.
Who is going to help us?

writing.prompt: Write five sentences about your friends, using a subject, an object, a possessive and a reflexive pronoun.
writing.example: They are my classmates. I help them. This idea is mine. We solved it ourselves.

micro_quiz.explanation: Subjects take 'He and I', with 'I' placed last for politeness.
After the preposition 'to', use the object pronoun 'me'.
'theirs' stands alone without a noun — a possessive pronoun.

challenge.q: Identify the error: 'The prize was shared between she and I.'
options: between she and I → her and me
challenge.explanation: After 'between' both pronouns must be objects: 'her and me'.

options: Each of the students have a desk.
Each of the students has a desk.
Each of the students have their desk.
Each of the student has a desk.

challenge.q: Choose the correct relative pronoun: 'The house ___ roof is red is ours.'
challenge.explanation: 'whose' shows possession (the roof belonging to the house).
